subtitre.subtitle: My name is Maria Velikanova, I am a psychologist, non-medical psychotherapist, and narrative practitioner. I work in two languages, Russian and French.I use these methods in my work:

texte.first: Narrative therapy helps in creating a 'preferred life story' with a focus on the client's own choices.
texte.second: Externalization of the problem is the work of seeing the problem as a separate phenomenon, not as part of the client's personality.
texte.third: Writing practices are structured techniques for gaining awareness and addressing issues.
texte.four: Art Therapy** – using creative expression (drawing, collage, music) as part of therapeutic work.

aboutpage.phrase: A lighthouse is not a port. Ships usually do not sail towards the lighthouse,but the lighthouse comes in the path of the ship in difficult moments, in a storm, in fog, when it is unclear where to sail, the path is indistinguishable, and obstacles seem insurmountable...
aboutpage.phrasedeux: This is how I see the role of the psychological practitioner. The lighthouse keeper is happy when the ship's captain, thanks to the light of the lighthouse, passes by the dangerous rocks and continues on his way toward the goal, without lingering near the lighthouse.

texteabout.firstabout:
I am a psychopractitioner, specializing in relational psychotherapy, narrative practices, and writing therapy. I work in two languages, Russian and French.

Before specializing in the field of psychotherapeutic support, I studied music (choir conducting) and literature.

I trained at the Institute of Consultative Psychology in person-centered therapy (Carl Rogers), followed by various trainings in writing therapy. I also worked with individuals in suicidal crisis as part of an in-depth internship for volunteers on the 'Choose Life' website, a Russian suicide prevention and awareness site that I founded and manage.

Currently, I continue to deepen my knowledge and specialize in the narrative approach, studying at the Institute for Online Psychological Practice 'The Future Today' (Moscow).

textedeux.textedeux:
I work with people who have experienced psychological trauma. I have worked for several years with people on the brink of suicide, so I have experience dealing with difficult emotional states.

I am a responsible person, and my responsibility includes not trying to work alone, say, with clinical depression requiring medical treatment. I will not refuse such a client, but I will agree to work only in collaboration with a doctor. I also believe that it is my responsibility to undergo personal therapy and supervision: the difficulties a psychologist, like any human being, faces in their life should not spill over into interactions with the client. That is why I currently have both a therapist and a supervisor.

I do not work with couples, children, or adult requests related to parenting.

However, I have experience working with parents of special children (children with developmental disorders).

My credo as a psychologist can be expressed in the phrase of the founder of logotherapy, Viktor Frankl: "So what is man? It is a being who always decides who he is."

I will never try to change you (it is not within my powers, nor anyone else's), I will not teach you, I will not lead you, because you are you, and you do not need to follow me, you have your own path. I believe that every person has a resource, an inner source, from which they can live their life, enjoying and bringing joy to others.

I consider that my role as a consulting psychologist is to walk alongside you, not ahead, sometimes offering my shoulder at difficult turns, being a helper on your path, until your legs become strong enough for an independent journey.

I live in France, in Metz, so I mainly use video consultations, sometimes chat and email. If you live in Western Europe, since mail works very quickly here, old-fashioned correspondence on paper is also possible. I trained at the Institute of Consultative Psychology in the person-centered approach (Carl Rogers), and then I followed several training courses in writing therapy. I also learned to work with people in suicidal crisis during an in-depth internship for volunteers at the Choose Life website, a Russian suicide prevention site created and run by me. All of this training was done in Moscow, Russia.

Right now, I continue to deepen my knowledge and skills, specializing in the narrative approach that I study at the Institute of Training in Psychological Practice online from the foundation "The Future Today" (Moscow).

I work with adults suffering from personal difficulties, loss of meaning, relational difficulties, depression, post-traumatic stress, pathological mourning. My volunteer experience on a suicide prevention site helps me work with suicidal crisis states or recovery after a suicide attempt. I am also interested in supporting parents who have a child with a mental disability or a psychological illness.

Thanks to my first two trainings, apart from dialogue, I use very varied forms of work, such as art therapy methods.

My credo could be summarized in the words of Viktor Frankl, the founder of logotherapy, a survivor of Auschwitz: "Everything can be taken from a man except one thing, the last of the human freedoms: to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances."

I will not attempt to change you (I could not, in fact, no one can change another, we can only change ourselves), I will not lecture you, I will not guide you, because you – you are you, and you must not follow me, you have your own path ahead of you. I believe that every human has an inner source from which they can draw strength to live their life joyfully.

I believe that my role as a helping relationship specialist is to walk beside you, not ahead, offering my help at complicated turns in the road, accompanying you on your journey until your legs become strong enough to continue without me.

I live in Metz, but I also consult via Skype, chat, email, phone, and even by correspondence.

first.title: Narrative Therapy
first.content: In my work, I practice the narrative approach. It is a new therapeutic approach that was created in the 1970s-1980s. Its authors are Australian social worker Michael White and New Zealand psychologist David Epston.

second.title: Externalization of the Problem
second.content: Externalization of the problem means separating the individual from the issue, presenting it as something external to them. This allows for a better understanding of the situation by distancing oneself from it, making it easier to find solutions.

third.title: Written Practices
third.content: Written practices involve exercises where the individual is encouraged to write down their thoughts, feelings, or reflections. This helps clarify ideas, organize emotions, and explore possible solutions to a problem.

four.title: Art Therapy
four.content: Art therapy uses creative processes, such as drawing or painting, to help individuals express their emotions and better understand their thoughts. It promotes healing by allowing patients to visualize and transform their inner experiences.

narrativetheraphie.textenarrative: Narrative Therapy is a form of psychotherapy that focuses on helping individuals separate themselves from their problems by viewing their experiences as stories. Developed by Michael White and David Epston, this approach emphasizes the importance of language and narrative in shaping our understanding of the world. It encourages people to externalize their issues, seeing them as separate from their identity. This allows clients to explore alternative narratives and find empowering meanings. Narrative Therapy helps individuals re-author their lives, highlighting strengths and values. It fosters a sense of agency and self-determination. By questioning dominant cultural narratives, clients can challenge limiting beliefs. This therapy is collaborative, treating the client as the expert of their own life. It is effective for a variety of issues, including trauma, anxiety, and identity struggles. Narrative Therapy promotes resilience by emphasizing personal agency and choice. It helps individuals see themselves as capable of change and growth.

textwritten.en: Written practices in narrative therapy encourage individuals to express their thoughts and feelings through writing. This method helps externalize internal experiences, creating a sense of distance and clarity. It allows clients to reflect on their stories and explore alternative perspectives. Writing also helps to organize complex emotions and events. It serves as a safe space for processing difficult experiences. Through journaling or letter-writing, individuals can engage in dialogues with different parts of themselves. This fosters self-awareness and emotional growth. Written practices are empowering as they allow clients to author their narratives. They can redefine their identity by highlighting strengths and values. This approach supports healing by transforming negative stories into empowering ones. It encourages resilience and personal agency. Writing also preserves important moments, helping individuals honor their journey. Narrative letters from therapists provide validation and encouragement. These letters serve as reminders of progress and achievements. Written practices are a powerful tool in building a positive self-image and moving forward with purpose.

arttheraphie.texteart: Art therapy is a creative approach to healing that helps individuals express their emotions through artistic mediums. It allows people to explore their inner thoughts and feelings without using words. Engaging in artistic creation fosters self-awareness and emotional release. Painting, drawing, and sculpting can help individuals process trauma and stress. Art therapy provides a non-judgmental space for self-expression. The creative process itself can be therapeutic and calming. It helps improve self-esteem by allowing individuals to see their personal growth. Art therapy is beneficial for both children and adults. It supports mental health by reducing anxiety and depression. This form of therapy is often used in hospitals, schools, and rehabilitation centers. Art can be a bridge between the conscious and unconscious mind. The use of colors and shapes helps reveal hidden emotions. Art therapy encourages resilience and problem-solving skills. Therapists guide clients to interpret their artwork and gain insight into their emotions. Creating art in a supportive environment fosters healing and personal transformation.

externalization.text: Externalization is a key concept in narrative therapy that helps individuals separate themselves from their problems. This approach allows people to see issues as external influences rather than internal flaws. By naming a problem, individuals can better understand and manage it. Externalization reduces feelings of guilt and self-blame. It encourages people to take control of their stories and redefine their identities. This method is especially useful in addressing anxiety, depression, and trauma. Therapists guide clients in personifying their problems, making them easier to analyze. By creating distance from the issue, individuals can find new perspectives and solutions. Externalization promotes resilience and self-compassion. It empowers people to challenge negative narratives that limit their growth. Writing, drawing, and storytelling can aid in the externalization process. This technique helps children and adults alike to cope with emotional struggles. Externalization is used in both individual and group therapy settings. It supports long-term emotional healing by fostering a sense of agency. Through externalization, people can rewrite their life stories in a way that reflects strength and hope.
